labels.why: A no vote on the postal overhaul could be about the cost of shifting retiree health costs to Medicare, not about running government well.
A no vote could be about adding a new immigration ban or about foreign policy, not about civil rights.
A no vote on the burn pit benefits bill could be about its cost or how it was budgeted.
A no vote could be about opposing new coverage mandates on insurers in general, not about making care affordable.
A no vote could be about the ten-year spending level or the wider eligibility rules, not about antipoverty aid itself.
A no vote could be about giving federal agencies new domestic surveillance roles, which is a civil liberties concern, not weaker public safety.
A no vote could be about the dedicated funding stream and how it was paid for.
A no vote could be about new bank rules or about adding a duty to the Federal Reserve, not about closing the wealth gap.
A no vote could be a judgment that this farm and biofuel spending would not actually lower prices.
A no vote could be about privacy or the burden of adding questions to federal surveys.
A no vote could be about creating a new federal alert system and coordinator, not about public safety goals.
A no vote on the final PACT Act could be about its cost or budget treatment.
No votes on a defense bill come from people who want less military spending and from people who object to other provisions in it.
A no vote could be about the spending level or the land management rules in the bill.
This bill bundled taxes, energy, and health together, so a no vote could be about the corporate tax or the overall spending.
A no vote could be about the tax and energy parts of the same bill rather than the drug pricing parts.
A no vote could be a preference for the separate Senate version of electoral count reform, or a federalism objection.
A no vote could be a judgment that grants to community groups are the wrong way to cut crime, not opposition to cutting crime.
A no vote could be about new federal grant spending or federal involvement in local policing.
A no vote could be about voiding contract terms people already signed, which is a contract law objection.
A no vote could be about funding community groups rather than about how to handle people leaving prison.
A no vote could be about extra paperwork for federal contractors, not about tolerating conflicts of interest.
A no vote could be about federal grants shaping local police training rather than about public safety.
A no vote could be about the privacy of tax returns or about the timing of this bill, not about corruption in general.
The whole resolution was to cancel a benefit program, so a no vote was the only way to keep it and cannot be explained by cost.
A no vote could be about disrupting small-business services by forcing offices to move, not about immigration policy.
A no vote could be about deferring to the President's trade authority, and saying someone opposes lower living costs would be wrong.
